Well it was first implemented in 2008 as a $10/tonne of CO2 tax, and then it increased yearly to $15, $20, $25 and then $30/tonne, which is the rate that it is currently frozen at. The current $30/tonne tax adds 6.7 cents to the price of a litre of gasoline, and applies to other fuel sources as well, with tax rates based on the amount of CO2 that they create. Currently the tax applies to 70% of all emissions in the region, since it would be more difficult to apply the tax to non-fuel-related agricultural emissions or deforestation.

The carbon tax has been billed as revenue-neutral, because all revenue from the tax has been returned to the public in the form of other tax cuts and grants. More specifically, the revenue has been used to reduce income taxes, reduce corporate taxes, send a tax-rebate to all low-income residents 4 times a year (along with GST rebates), and provide a grant to all rural residents.

The key concept and reasoning behind the carbon tax is that air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions are a negative externality, which harms other parties, but will not be properly taken into account in an individual's decision-making. This results in a market failure, where markets will over-produce goods which cause harm to people outside of the transaction (everyone other than the buyer or the seller), since the buyer and seller will be acting in their own self-interest, and not fully considering their impact on everyone else. The carbon tax is meant to account for those external impacts, to bring an individual's private costs of polluting more in line with the full costs to society.

At the same time, it’s been extraordinarily effective in tackling the root cause of carbon pollution: the burning of fossil fuels. Since the tax came in, fuel use in the region has dropped by 16 percent; in the rest of the country, it’s risen by 3 percent (counting all fuels covered by the tax). To put that accomplishment in perspective, the national Kyoto target was a 6-percent reduction in 20 years. And the evidence points to the carbon tax as the major driver of these regional gains.

Further, while some had predicted that the tax shift would hurt the province’s economy, in fact, the region’s GDP has slightly outperformed the rest of the country’s since 2008.

This understanding offers us a fairly straightforward idea of moral progress: it means including ever more people (or beings) in the group of those whose interests are to be respected. This too is an ancient insight: a Stoic philosopher of the second century describes us as being surrounded by a series of concentric circles. The innermost circle of concern surrounds our own self; the next comprises the immediate family; then follow more remote family; then, in turn, neighbours, fellow community members, countrymen and, finally, the human race as a whole. The philosopher described moral progress as ‘drawing the circles somehow toward the centre’, or moving members of outer circles to the inner ones.

We can see the moral progress of recent centuries in these terms: we have witnessed an extension of the circle of respect and concern to various groups such as women, marginalized communities, and LGBTQ+ individuals. And in these terms, we have come a long way. But it is equally clear that there is room for improvement. Part of imagining what future generations will condemn us for is therefore imagining how the circle might widen further.

We can also turn our question around and ask, what will future generations admire us for? When we look back, we admire those who courageously challenged the norms of their day, such as prominent activists and leaders who widened the circle of moral concern. We have the chance to do that, too. And if we manage, then perhaps future generations will forgive us our sins.

This article is not specific to any one country, but I think it offers a lot of compelling ideas for us to consider, and it raises questions that force us to step back and consider the implications of our society's practices from a distance.

For the sake of sparking conversation, I'll post a passage of each of the main ideas separately here, since they're each worthy of their own discussion.

1) Rights for future generations. Currently, only people alive now can claim rights. But just as we have extended our circle of moral concern among the living, so it can be extended in time. The problem is clear: we often make decisions that will have impacts on people far into the future – such as producing nuclear waste that will remain toxic for millions of years – yet those future people are not here to stand up for themselves. Neither defining nor granting these rights will be easy. But there are precedents on which we can draw, such as the ways we protect the rights of small children or animals, who also cannot speak for themselves.

So our successors will have to be imaginative in creating a framework robust enough to defend the unborn in the face of the interests of those alive today, with which they often conflict. For we should be under no illusions: to take the rights of future generations seriously would involve massive restrictions on our freedom of action. Currently, we despoil the earth and seas with impunity to enjoy a luxurious lifestyle (by historical standards). In 100 years, this will be seen as wickedness comparable to colonial powers despoiling their colonies. Though our successors will be appalled by our consumerism, we will not find it easy to adjust to more modest ways.

Rights for other conscious beings. This too is a plausible extension of the circle of moral concern, and one that is already underway. It is no longer in doubt that non-human animals feel pain and indeed many more complex emotions too. They therefore clearly have interests, such as to run free, or pursue social interactions appropriate for their species. To take account of the interests only of humans and not of other animals is therefore increasingly regarded as speciesism – an unjustified discrimination akin to racism or sexism.

The situation for other species is dire: humans have never raised so many animals for slaughter – five times as many today as in the mid-20th century – while our impact on the environment is causing other species to become extinct a thousand times faster than normal. There will be many difficult decisions ahead as we try to balance human interests against those of other creatures, or the interests of individual animals against the species or the ecosystem. But our descendants will not excuse us for failing to make these decisions just because they are difficult. More likely, they will curse us for killing all the rhinos, and find our consumption of factory-farmed products as morally repulsive as we now find cannibalism.

As soon as our computers become conscious – and they will – then this extension of concern will apply to them, too.

Wards vs At-Large voting is an interesting question, and there's definite pros and cons to each. Wards allow for representation closer to the people, but potentially lead to councillors focusing too much on the interests of their neighbourhood and ignoring the impact on others (and thus more NIMBYism and political fights between different neighbourhoods). At-Large voting allows councillors to consider the big picture instead of just the needs of their own neighbourhood, but it also makes it more difficult for independents or lesser-known candidates to get elected through grassroots campaigns, and means less direct representation for people.

I really don't know what I'd prefer. I currently like the way the current system reduces the amount of neighbourhood politics and allows councillors to focus on the big picture and get things done, but I do see real merits in having a ward-based system, and understand the concerns that the current system makes local politics overwhelming for most voters (how can they possibly have an opinion about so many candidates?), and thus has negative impacts on voter engagement and their representation.

Interestingly, there have been five referendums/plebiscites on this topic since 1970:

1973: 59 percent of voters chose to keep the at-large system.

1978: 52 percent voted in favour of reinstating a ward system. However, the provincial government's amendments to the local charter, the legislation that governs the city, specified that the electoral system could only be changed with a 60 percent majority vote in a referendum.

1988: 56 percent majority in favour of wards, which was not enough to meet the 60 percent required.

1996: 59 percent voted in favour of keeping the at-large system.

2004: 54 percent voted opposed to adopting a ward system.

How inefficient climate policies can build support for efficient ones

A carbon tax is a paradigmatic wide policy — it sends a weak signal to the entire economy. Policies in that country began with funding for research and development, then subsidies for demonstration projects during the 1970s and 1980s, and continued to larger-scale market formation programs, including a feed-in law after a major nuclear disaster. These policies led to industrial expansion in wind and, later, solar energy production; these developments helped create and expand a coalition of interests that fought to defend existing measures and supported further measures.

For all the hassle that country sometimes gets from analysts, it has sequenced its climate policies brilliantly. Each one creates more industries and constituencies that support further policy expansion.

Economists view green industrial policies as third- or fourth-best options for efficiency. I find it interesting that most people arguing against a referendum are basically arguing against democracy.

Not at all. Voting for a representative is very different from voting on a specific topic.

Most people are interested and knowledgeable about *some* topics, but very few people are interested and knowledgeable about *every* topic. When voting for political parties and representatives, people can use the issues that they know and care most about to decide which party best matches their views and values.

So for example, if I know lots about economic and environmental policy, but only have a shallow understanding of foreign policy, it's okay because I can judge the parties based on their economic and environmental policies, which are issues that I do understand.

However with a referendum, we're relying on *everyone* to be knowledgeable, interested, and informed about the same topic. If it's a topic with any complexity (like electoral reform), then that won't necessarily work very well, because let's be honest: most people are not going to approach the topic with an open mind and spend 3+ hours independently researching it, and weighing the tradeoffs and potential implications. Most will hear about it on the news a few times, hear an argument that they like, and vote accordingly. This also makes it very easy for many people to be convinced by misleading information, because they're not experts on the topic, and most people don't have the time or interest to develop a very thorough understanding of the topic before voting.

Basically, the countries in a certain European agreement have no border controls between themselves, so people and goods can move freely between them without any waits, and without needing to bring a passport. So for example, you can drive or take a train from one country to another without going through any border stops, or you can fly between those countries without going through customs. It also speeds up goods movement, since trucks and freight trains don't have to wait in border lines and get searched every time they cross a national border.
